meta.title: Who really said "Writing is easy. All you do is stare at a blank sheet of paper until drops of blood form on your forehead"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Douglas Adams. It is a newsroom joke: credited to Gene Fowler since 1980, and printed in Time in 1961 as Red Smith's. No Adams source exists.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Writing is easy. All you do is stare at a blank sheet of paper until drops of blood form on your forehead'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Douglas Adams. A newsroom joke credited to Gene Fowler from 1980, and printed in Time in 1961 as Red Smith's line. No source in Adams's work.

answer.label: Not Douglas Adams — a newsroom joke, credited to Gene Fowler
answer.authorDates: 1890–1960 · American newspaperman, biographer and Hollywood screenwriter
answer.sourceLine: A 1980 quotation anthology, The Writer’s Quotation Book, printed a version of this line under Gene Fowler’s name with no citation attached — the first known Fowler credit, and Fowler had died in 1960. The exact wording used here is the one that circulates today, and it is traceable no further back than a 2000 writing manual, again uncited. The earliest printing of the blood-on-the-forehead image is older still and belongs to someone else: Time reported it on 1 September 1961 as a line of the sports columnist Red Smith. No Adams source has ever been produced — the one recording in which he uses the line has him crediting Ring Lardner.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Writer’s Quotation Book: A Literary Companion (1980), ed. James Charlton
Time, 1 September 1961 — the same joke, credited to sportswriter Red Smith

source.excerpt: Red is not wide-eyed about the world of sports… But like all good writers in any field, he takes sportswriting in dead earnest. “Writing a column is easy,” he once said. “You just sit at your typewriter until little drops of blood appear on your forehead.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the whole family: Paul Gallico in print in 1946, Red Smith via Walter Winchell’s column in 1949, the first forehead version in Time on 1 September 1961, “beads of blood” in The Rotarian in June 1963, and the first credit to Gene Fowler in a 1980 quotation anthology. Douglas Adams is not mentioned anywhere in the article.

Wikiquote’s Gene Fowler page ↗ prints this exact wording, marks it as attributed without citation in Janice R. Matthews et al., Successful Scientific Writing (2000), p. 53, and appends the line “Sometimes attributed to Douglas Adams.”

Wikiquote’s Douglas Adams page ↗ has no such quotation anywhere in it; the talk page ↗ preserves the removal, with an editor noting that Adams himself used the line in a recorded talk and credited Ring Lardner for it.

Wikipedia’s Gene Fowler article ↗ lists the line under “Memorable quotations” with no citation of any kind attached — which is the whole difficulty: every modern printing points back to another modern printing.
source.excerptNote: Time, 1 September 1961, on the columnist Red Smith, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. This is the earliest instance of the blood-on-the-forehead image in that chronology. The smoother “Writing is easy… blank sheet of paper” form that circulates under Douglas Adams’s name appears nineteen years later, in a 1980 anthology, credited to Gene Fowler.

source.rightsNote: No first publication can be identified for this wording, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted. What is documented is a chain of secondary printings — a 1961 magazine report of a spoken remark, a 1980 quotation anthology, later reference works — none of which is a work by the person credited, and any rights in the underlying columns or books would rest with their own authors and publishers rather than with the floating quip.

author.name: Gene Fowler
author.kicker: The name the joke usually lands on
author.heading: Who Gene Fowler actually was
author.metaLine: 1890–1960 · Denver Post and New York newspaperman, biographer, screenwriter
author.bio: Gene Fowler was born in Denver in 1890 and died in West Los Angeles in 1960. He came up through The Denver Post and a run of New York papers — the Daily Mirror, the Evening Journal, the New York American, The Morning Telegraph — then became one of the highest-paid screenwriters in 1930s and 1940s Hollywood, with credits including What Price Hollywood? and The Call of the Wild. He wrote biographies of John Barrymore, Mack Sennett and Jimmy Durante, and the memoir Skyline; the quips about writing that carry his name today are mostly attached to him by later anthologists rather than found in those books.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented instance of the blood-on-the-forehead wording: “Writing a column is easy… You just sit at your typewriter until little drops of blood appear on your forehead,” credited to Red Smith in “The Press: Good Sports,” Time, 1 September 1961. A version of this wording first appears credited to Gene Fowler in James Charlton, ed., The Writer’s Quotation Book: A Literary Companion (1980), which prints it as “Writing is easy; all you do is sit staring at the blank sheet of paper until the drops of blood form on your forehead.” The wording quoted here is attested no earlier than Janice R. Matthews et al., Successful Scientific Writing (2000), p. 53, again without citation. Both earlier citations as documented in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: Writing Is Easy; You Just Open a Vein and Bleed” (14 September 2011).

copyAttribution: Not Douglas Adams. "Writing is easy. All you do is stare at a blank sheet of paper until drops of blood form on your forehead" is newsroom shop talk: a version of it first appears credited to Gene Fowler (1890–1960) in a 1980 quotation anthology, without a source, this exact wording is attested no earlier than a 2000 writing manual, again uncited, and the earliest printing of the blood-on-the-forehead image is in Time on 1 September 1961, where it is credited to the sports columnist Red Smith. No source in Douglas Adams's work has ever been found. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been handed this joke
misattribution.intro: This is one of the great free-floating quips: a gag about the pain of writing that attaches itself to whichever famous writer the reader already associates with suffering at a desk. Quote Investigator tracks it across at least five names, and Douglas Adams is a late arrival whom no reference work supports — Wikiquote records the Adams credit only as a note (“Sometimes attributed to Douglas Adams”) on Gene Fowler’s page, and its Douglas Adams page removed the line entirely.

items.scope: the whole line, in several wordings
items.why: Nothing in Adams’s books, columns or interviews has been shown to contain it. Wikiquote’s Adams page ↗ does not carry the line, and its talk page ↗ records an editor deleting it, on the grounds that in a recorded talk Adams uses the joke but says “I think it comes from Ring Lardner.” That is an editor’s note rather than a verdict, but it points the same way as everything else: Adams was passing the line on, not coining it.

The standard correction, and still not a sourced one. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the first Fowler credit in The Writer’s Quotation Book: A Literary Companion (1980); Fowler died in 1960. Wikiquote prints the line as attributed without citation, and Wikipedia lists it among his “memorable quotations” with nothing attached.

items.scope: “It is easy to write. Just sit in front of your typewriter and bleed.”
items.why: Quote Investigator calls this credit implausible: the earliest known ascription to Hemingway is in The Craft of Fiction (1973), a how-to book for aspiring authors, and Hemingway died in 1961 ↗, with the saying already in circulation.

items.scope: “Just put a sheet of paper in the typewriter and start bleeding.”
items.why: First credited to Wolfe in Gene Olson’s Sweet Agony (1972), many years after his death and with no supporting evidence. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes there is no substantive evidence connecting the saying to either Wolfe or Hemingway.

misattribution.truthLine: The image is newsroom property, not literary property. Quote Investigator ↗ gives chronological precedence to Paul Gallico in 1946 for the modern metaphor, credits Red Smith with the famous 1949 version, and notes that the status of the later blood-on-the-forehead variants — the ones this page is about — is simply not clear.

context.heading: Why this one keeps landing on Douglas Adams
lead: Adams is a magnet for writing jokes because he genuinely was the funniest procrastinator in English letters, and he said so himself — Wikiquote sources “I love deadlines. I love the whooshing noise they make as they go by” ↗ to The Salmon of Doubt (2002). Once a writer owns that reputation, every gag about the agony of the blank page drifts toward his name, and the drift is one-way: nobody ever moves a joke from Douglas Adams to a dead Denver newspaperman.

The line itself started somewhere far less literary. It is sportswriters’ shop talk about filing a daily column, and its documented history runs through Paul Gallico’s Confessions of a Story Writer in 1946 and Walter Winchell’s column in 1949, where Red Smith is asked whether turning out a column is a chore and dead-pans that you simply sit down at the typewriter, open your veins, and bleed ↗. The blood-on-the-forehead version is a later refinement of the same joke.
context.detailsSummary: The chronology, as Quote Investigator documents it
detailsBody: 1946 — Paul Gallico, Confessions of a Story Writer: “It is only when you open your veins and bleed onto the page a little that you establish contact with your reader.” Quote Investigator calls this the modern metaphorical form.
1949 — Walter Winchell’s syndicated column reports Red Smith’s dead-pan version. 1961 — Time prints the first forehead variant, again as Smith’s. 1963 — The Rotarian runs it as “beads of blood.”

1972 and 1973 — the joke is handed posthumously to Thomas Wolfe and then to Ernest Hemingway. 1980 — a quotation anthology gives the polished “Writing is easy… blank sheet of paper” wording to Gene Fowler, the first known Fowler credit. The hop to Douglas Adams is later still, and no reference work supports it — Wikiquote carries it only as a “sometimes attributed” note on Fowler’s page, and struck it from Adams’s own.
context.pull: I love deadlines. I love the whooshing noise they make as they go by.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Douglas Adams. Conventionally credited to Gene Fowler, but that credit is unsourced and first appears in a 1980 quotation anthology, twenty years after his death; Quote Investigator concludes the status of the blood-on-the-forehead wording is not clear.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's chronology gives: Gallico 1946, Winchell/Red Smith 1949, Time 1 Sept 1961 for the first 'drops of blood... forehead' version credited to Smith, The Rotarian June 1963 'beads of blood', Olson's Sweet Agony 1972 crediting Thomas Wolfe, Knott's The Craft of Fiction 1973 crediting Hemingway (who died in 1961), and The Writer's Quotation Book (1980) as the first known credit to Gene Fowler. QI concludes the status of the forehead variants is not clear, and never mentions Douglas Adams.

Wikiquote's Gene Fowler page prints 'Writing is easy. All you do is stare at a blank sheet of paper until drops of blood form on your forehead', marks it 'Attributed without citation in Janice R. Matthews et al. (2000) Successful Scientific Writing. p. 53', and adds 'Sometimes attributed to Douglas Adams'. It also gives Fowler's dates as 8 March 1890 – 2 July 1960.

Wikiquote's Douglas Adams page contains no blood/forehead/blank-sheet quotation anywhere, has no Misattributed or Disputed section, gives Adams's dates as 11 March 1952 – 11 May 2001, and lists 'I love deadlines. I love the whooshing noise they make as they go by' in its The Salmon of Doubt (2002) section.

Talk:Douglas Adams contains a section headed '"Writing is easy..."' in which an editor records removing the line from the article, stating that Adams uses the quote in a linked video but also says 'I think it comes from Ring Lardner', and noting the quote is often attributed to Gene Fowler.

Wikipedia's Gene Fowler article gives his dates as 8 March 1890 (Denver) – 2 July 1960 (West Los Angeles), describes his career at The Denver Post and New York papers and as a highly paid Hollywood screenwriter, and prints the quote under a 'Memorable quotations' heading with no citation attached.

Wikipedia's Red Smith article gives his full name as Walter Wellesley Smith, dates 25 September 1905 – 15 January 1982, a 1976 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary, and the 1949 Winchell-reported 'open your veins, and bleed' line; it does not contain a forehead version.
Google Books returns a page-56 snippet from The Rotarian containing 'beads of blood form on my forehead', on a page whose text also mentions Red Smith.
